headline: Munar recovers from a lost tiebreak to knock No. 3 seed Fritz out of Tokyo
dek: Jaume Munar won 6-7(7), 6-4, 6-3 in round 1 of the ATP 500 in Tokyo, three days after starting in qualifying.

paragraphs: For most of an hour in Tokyo, the opening round looked like it would follow the script that Taylor Fritz has written for years: hold the tight moments, take the first set, and close. Jaume Munar, who had to come through qualifying just to reach the main draw, refused to let that script finish, and turned a lost tiebreak into the biggest result of his week.
It was not supposed to be close on paper. Fritz arrived as the No. 3 seed and ranked No. 10 at the start of the week; Munar was unseeded at No. 66.

sections.heading: A tiebreak lost, then a different match
paragraphs: The first set went the distance and then some. Neither man could separate before the tiebreak, and Fritz needed a 9-7 tiebreak to take it. For a player who had already spent two matches in qualifying, dropping a set that long could have been the end of the story.

Instead the match changed shape. Munar took the second set 6-4, the first time all afternoon that the scoreboard tilted his way, and the third was cleaner still at 6-3. Losing the opener and then winning the next two sets is exactly the pattern Fritz rarely allows, which is why the order of the sets matters more here than the final line.

The sets tell the swing on their own. This was a match that grew less tight as it went on: a first set that needed an extended tiebreak, a second set that went the distance on games, and a third that Munar closed with room to spare. Fritz never led again after the opener.
sections.visual_note: Read the sets from top to bottom: the only set Fritz won needed an extended tiebreak, while Munar's two sets were each settled on games alone. The match did not drift away from Fritz in one swing; it closed on him set by set.

sections.heading: What the records said going in
paragraphs: Little in Munar's results suggested this kind of afternoon. He was 4-20 against top-10 players before Tokyo and had won 45.3% of his matches, while Fritz had won 62.1% of his across a far longer career at the top of the game.

The detail that makes the comeback unusual sits in Fritz's own profile. When he wins the opening set he goes on to win the match 86% of the time, which is what made a lost first set feel decisive for Munar. Coming back from a set down had not been Munar's habit either, so this ran against both men's history at once.
sections.visual_note: These bars are each player's results before the match, not this match's numbers. Fritz leads almost every line, which is the point: the result came against the grain, above all on matches won from a set down.

sections.heading: Three wins before the main draw had properly begun
paragraphs: The win also capped a demanding start to the week. Munar opened qualifying by recovering from a set down against Marcos Giron, winning 5-7 6-1 6-4, and then beat Aleksandar Kovacevic 6-2 6-3 to reach the main draw. Fritz, meanwhile, was playing his first match of the tournament.

Munar was not a fresh name ambushing a seed; he was a player who had already come back once that week and knew what a lost opening set felt like. His results just before Tokyo had been uneven, with a five-set win over Terence Atmane at the US Open followed by a straight-sets loss to Arthur Rinderknech, so the Tokyo run is a sharper stretch than anything just before it.
sections.visual_note: The path shows two qualifying wins before the Fritz match, the first of them also won after losing the opening set. Every result here is from this week, so the column tells the story of this run rather than of the season.

sections.heading: What it opens up
paragraphs: Removing the No. 3 seed in the first round changes the shape of that section of the draw. Munar's next opponent is Jaime Faria in round 2, a match in which he will be the more established name in the pairing rather than the outsider he was against Fritz.

It also adds to a stretch in which Munar has kept finding his way through long matches. The five-set win over Atmane in New York came from two sets down, and in Tokyo he has now won twice in a week after losing the opening set, a different profile from the one his comeback numbers describe.

For Fritz, the loss is a single result against a long run of reliable ones, and he wins most matches like this. For Munar, the question for the rest of the week is whether a qualifier who has now won three matches in Tokyo can keep turning close sets his way without a long tiebreak taking the first one from him again.
